title: Calcutta HC: Second Suit Over Same Share Deal Barred, Not a Commercial Dispute Either
meta_description: Calcutta High Court holds a fraud suit over cancelled share agreements barred under Order II Rule 2(3) CPC, wrongly sent to the Commercial Division.
bench: Justices Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya and Sandip Kumar De
case_name: Funidea Projects Private Limited & Anr. v. Dr. Dilip Kumar Ghosh & Ors.
citation: Division Bench ruling reported 14 October 2026; exact neutral citation not independently confirmed
body: Dr Dilip Kumar Ghosh and Kamala Ghosh ran into the oldest problem in civil litigation strategy: filing a second suit when the first one has not yet run its course and covers much of the same ground. Back in 2015 they had filed a money suit against Funidea Projects seeking unpaid consideration under a set of share transfer agreements. Years later, with that suit still pending, they filed a fresh suit asking for the same agreements to be cancelled outright, this time on allegations of fraud. The Calcutta High Court's Division Bench was not inclined to let the second suit proceed.

The bench, comprising Justices Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya and Sandip Kumar De, held that the later suit was barred by Order II Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and by the doctrine of election. Once a plaintiff has sued on part of a claim arising from one cause of action, the rule generally requires the entire claim to be brought in that suit, and a plaintiff who elects to pursue one remedy, here a money claim for consideration due, cannot later turn around and pursue an inconsistent remedy, here cancellation of the very agreements that consideration was payable under, in a separate proceeding.

What made the ruling useful beyond this particular pair of litigants was the court's approach to when such a bar can be decided without a trial. The bench held that where a plain reading of the plaint, together with the documents it relies on, discloses the ingredients of the Order II Rule 2(3) bar, the plaint should be rejected at the threshold rather than allowed to proceed to evidence. No fact-finding exercise is needed when the bar is apparent on the face of the pleadings and the documents annexed to them, and sending such a suit to trial only delays the inevitable.

The same bench also dealt with a second, separately significant point. The suit had been transferred to the Calcutta High Court's Commercial Division on the footing that it involved a shareholders' agreement dispute, which qualifies as a commercial dispute under Section 2(1)(c)(xii) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. The court disagreed, holding that a share purchase agreement does not become a shareholders' agreement merely because it concerns the transfer of shares. The two instruments serve different purposes, and the transfer to the Commercial Division was set aside along with the dismissal of the suit on the Order II Rule 2(3) point.

Both findings travel together in a way that matters for drafting and forum strategy. A litigant who wants the procedural advantages of the Commercial Courts Act, faster timelines, mandatory case management, and a bench accustomed to commercial disputes, cannot get there simply by labelling an ordinary share sale and purchase dispute as a shareholders' agreement matter. The court is prepared to look past the label to the substance of what the agreement actually does.

For transactional lawyers advising on exits and share sales, the ruling is a caution about structuring claims when a counterparty defaults on consideration and the underlying commercial relationship later turns adversarial. A client who sues first for the money and later discovers grounds to allege fraud in the underlying transaction cannot treat those as two bites at the same cherry filed years apart. The fraud allegation, if there is one, needs to be brought in the same proceeding as the money claim, or pleaded as an amendment to it, rather than packaged as a fresh suit once the first one is already underway and its outcome uncertain.

The practical message for anyone drafting a plaint off the back of a soured share transaction is to decide, before filing, exactly what relief is being sought and bring every available ground for it in one go. Splitting a single commercial grievance into a money suit now and a cancellation suit later invites exactly the threshold dismissal that Ghosh and his co-plaintiff received here, and no amount of later-discovered fraud allegation will rescue a claim that should have been pleaded the first time around.
why_it_matters: The ruling gives defendants a sharper tool to kill a second, overlapping suit at the threshold rather than fighting it through trial, provided the bar under Order II Rule 2(3) is apparent from the plaint and its annexed documents. It also narrows what counts as a shareholders' agreement dispute for Commercial Courts Act purposes, denying litigants an easy route to that forum merely by invoking share transfer language. Both points will be cited in future motions to dismiss and in jurisdictional objections raised in share-sale disputes across Indian commercial courts.
card_summary: Calcutta HC throws out a second suit over cancelled share agreements as barred under Order II Rule 2(3) CPC, and rules a share purchase agreement is not a shareholders' agreement under the Commercial Courts Act.
card_tip: Plead every relief arising from one transaction in a single suit; a later suit seeking an inconsistent remedy on the same facts risks dismissal at the threshold without trial.
verification_notes: The core holdings on Order II Rule 2(3), the threshold-dismissal standard, and the share purchase agreement versus shareholders' agreement distinction are confirmed by both Law Street and LiveLawBiz, which report the same bench and the same underlying 2015 money suit background. The exact neutral citation is not stated because the two case-law trackers located (courtkutchehry.com) list conflicting citation numbers for this judgment, and that discrepancy could not be resolved from available sources, so no specific citation number is asserted. The precise date of the 2015 money suit filing and the quantum of unpaid consideration claimed were not independently confirmed beyond being described as a 2015 filing, so no amount is stated.
